main_review: Though I haven't seen all of Nolan's films, I have greatly enjoyed what I have seen so far (Insomnia, the Batman trilogy, and Inception), and with sci-fi being one of my favourite genres, seeing 'Interstellar' eventually was a no-brainer for me. Despite its 169 minutes, it didn't seem long at all (if a film is well made, then the longer, the better) and it's resoundingly clear that Christopher is excellent both in getting fine performances from his actors and, along with his brother Jonathan, in writing scripts. What makes the film special for a sci-fi work is that he doesn't have to show any monster--nothing is truly more scary than humanity itself. This is a work that can combine an excellent explanation of the theory of relativity yet still show that the only things that truly matter are the relationships we develop in our everyday lives. My favourite film of all-time is still one of the most ambitious, '2001: A Space Odyssey', but it's very comforting to me that six generations after the birth of cinema, and the Faberge eggs of genius that have come along the way, from Georges Méliès' 'A Trip to the Moon' and Fritz Lang's 'Metropolis', that outstanding works of science fiction, such as 'Gravity', 'Ex Machina' and this fine film by Nolan, are still being made. There's hope for us yet!...

Brothers Christopher and Jonathan Nolan wrote the screenplay, which has its origins in a script Jonathan developed in 2007. Christopher Nolan produced the film with his wife Emma Thomas through their production company Syncopy and with Lynda Obst through Lynda Obst Productions. Caltech theoretical physicist Kip Thorne, whose work inspired the film, was an executive producer and acted as scientific consultant. Warner Bros., Paramount Pictures, and Legendary Pictures co-financed the film.

Reviews: Underwhelming and at the best okay.
main_review: I went into this film expecting great things, especially with Christopher Nolan's film Inception being one of the best films put to screen in recent years it's just a shame that it felt like someone filmed a glacier. You watch on in awe of the visuals before you and the way it's been filmed draws you into the people there and you wonder what it would be like to see what they did for yourself. Reviews: Outstanding, an example for other writers to learn from
main_review: I cannot help but compare this to 2001, A Space Odyssey: That Christopher Nolan has produced something that can compare to the work of Clarke & Kubrick is the highest praise I can think of for anything in this genre since.While 2001 has in many respects a more complex plot, Interstellar achieves a very similar depth while not seeming derivative. Few movies have approached the detail in 2001 when it comes to things like portrayal of gravity in space - this is one. As in 2001, the visual effects are excellent but serve to deliver the film rather than carry it.Interstellar packs a nicely mind-bending plot, plenty of appeal in a general sci-fi sense, and good attention to detail in those aspects of sci-fi that can in fact be realistic: thrusters not making noise in vacuum, for instance.It isn't "hard sci-fi" to the level that 2001 was, but it doesn't at all suffer from that distinction -- the aspects that may be completely unrealistic are portrayed such that they don't interfere with enjoying the film.Many details that would need reconciliation with realism are conveyed in a manner that seems well done and not cheap as in some films (Event Horizon, while by no means in the same class, is an example of what I mean). There are things that aren't explained (and would be tough to explain convincingly) and Nolan expertly diverts the viewer to the rest of the story rather than giving a contrived explanation of why things work the way they do.The acting is superb, the characters are believable (not to mention much more human than those in 2001), and overall I would say this is the best science fiction movie I've seen in at least a decade.Is it a better film than 2001? No. However, I'm not certain that 2001 is a better film than Interstellar. They are similar in some respects, but different in enough that they both stand as excellent in their own right.

Reviews: I would say a philosophical movie, not a SF one
main_review: First and foremost, I have to say the premise of the movie is really a philosophical one disguised as a science-fiction one, as far as I'm concerned.Secondly, I don't really care about the absolute groundwork of physics in movies, because that's not the important part - so I basically ignore any "problems" with the scientific part that some people are so obsessed (and wrongly so, from my perspective) - about. But going back to the premise of the movie, which is that some things transcend the confinements of the 4-dimensional reality - THAT is what I really enjoyed.In fact, such concepts have been pretty successfully grasped for quite some time, and are not exactly science-fiction. One example is the Kaluza-Klein theory.The conclusion? I have to say that even during watching the movie I've had quite a few personal epiphanies that will remain personal. Nothing to change my mind, just additional fuel to confirm what I've been knowing for quite some time, and with each additional evidence and with each additional piece, the more I'm certain that what I believe is correct. Thing is, I didn't need any of this, but it is refreshing to see that the movie creators feel the same.The point of the movie is not about science, is not about technology, is not about space, is not about even philosophy itself. The point of the movie is about realizing what is important in YOUR life. I know this seems like stretching a movie for the sake of personal connectivity with it, but I really believe the point of the movie is to make you understand what is important in your life and how sometimes what feels hopeless is doable, is possible, and can be made.It might look impossible, it might be complex, it might be difficult, it might take a long time - but assuming you don't give up on it and assuming it's really important to you - maybe that thing does indeed transcend the normal dimensions of space and time not because it's supernatural, but because some things are really underestimated, like the power of love.I'll let you think about what that something is for YOU, anybody who reads this.

At what point does humanity cease when we struggle to survive?These questions are something that could only be presented this well in the context of this film and in the hands of capable writers and the director - they give us no answer. We are meant to infer these meanings and all the while feel ourselves sink into the world being created for us. main_review: I have to preface this in saying I went into this film expecting a lot of exactly what I got, but it was what I didn't expect that really got me excited. The film succeeds absolutely with its brilliant visual effects, which in addition to being intense, dynamic and dazzling, focuses on the level of scientific realism agreed upon between director and theoretical physicist executive producer Kip Thorne. Although the visuals could drive the film without relying on quick cuts but beautiful vistas, stocked with bleak representation of Dust Bowl imagery, they are not even half of what had me enamored with the film. Fully expecting what I saw, I was thrilled with what I saw of the cinematography, but the humanity that I also saw had me wondering who's film i was in. Interstellar incorporates all of the cerebral, mind-bending inner workings of Inception, but without the odd aura of disaffectedness surrounding every character and plot event. In essence, Interstellar is all of the epic sound-scape and ever-compounding plot structure that Inception tries to be, yet with characters, or at least situations, that actually stand to move the audience. Time is a big theme in the film, so much so, and in such a similar fashion as Inception, that Interstellar almost seems to be Nolan's attempt to right the wrongs of Inception's faulty promises, and what we get is a complex story that we not only are able to understand, but are implored to listen to. Matthew McConaughy is pretty good, and the rest of the ensemble is passable enough. The slew of references toward Star Wars, 2001: A Space Odyssey and others are consistent and entertaining enough to keep film buffs intrigued, and for once, I felt anything but cheated coming out of this film, a perfect balancing show of personal and societal concerns in a Hollywood film, a test of only their greatest screenwriters for the contemporary blockbuster film.

Imagine Gravity and 2001 - A Space Odyssey had a baby; they'd name it Interstellar. With the production values of both and with science and nature not fantasy-magic driving the awe and wonder Interstellar leaves a long, lingering taste in your head.Matthew McConaughey plays ex-NASA pilot turned farmer in some recognisably normal version of the Earth's future. We're just a few years ahead of our now and terrible climatic change is wreaking havoc with our ability to produce enough food. America is pedalling backwards, people are returning to the land in a desperate attempt to grow enough food but it is clear we are in the end of days of the human race. Cooper (McConaughey's character) is a widower, raising a teenage son and daughter. The daughter, Murphy, is intellectually gifted and in the early part of the narrative experiences poltergeist-type activity in her bedroom; things gets broken, books get pushed off shelves, strange lines appear on the floor when dust from a storm swills into her room. These lines turn out to be a simple binary code, co-ordinates of a secret NASA facility which Cooper sets off one night to investigate. Enter Michael Caine and NASA's skeleton crew, the once great and good space agency reduced to skulking in a mountain-side because public opinion, with the Earth going to hell in a hand-cart, not supportive of grand spending on the so-called folly of space exploration.Michael Caine's character, a gifted physicist called Professor Brand who Cooper knows from when he worked for NASA, has a grand vision for the future of humanity. He also has some of the best lines, several of which turn up in the trailers. You'll know the one I mean; "Mankind was born on Earth, we were never meant to die here." Having discovered this mission to save the Earth Cooper learns of a stable worm-hole that has appeared in the orbit of Saturn which offers humans the opportunity to travel in interstellar space to search out a new home. His mission with a team of other astronauts, one of which is Professor Brand's daughter (played by Anne Hathaway), is to travel through the worm-hole to connect up with several pioneer missions that have already journeyed interstellar. NASA has lost contact with them though.Enough plot to get you started I think, anymore begins to damage the sheer joy and wonder of a beautifully constructed story. Interstellar is science-fiction rooted deeply in science fact, it represents Einstein's relativity in narrative form, showing fascinatingly the time-bending qualities of dense gravitational fields. We have a black hole, a singularity and theories of everything. Interstellar bends narrative, back upon itself - lose not sight of that poltergeist - as well as space-time (as relativity predicts) along with our minds. Great story, great performances and cinema as it should be. Space is experienced as deadly, beautiful and silent. The forces that shape our Universe are portrayed superbly and the ridiculously puny nature of our lives is writ large.Interstellar is definitely the best rendition of theoretical physics on the big screen, a physicist, Kip Thorne was on board as a consultant and producer. It's been generally well-received by critics and justifiably so. It would be my film of the year so far. Story, script and science beautifully intermingled and not an alien in sight. The one sour note in the reviews was Peter Bradshaw's in the Guardian. I love the Guardian but it does have on the payroll a cast of intellectual-snobs whose main role in life seems to be to sneer and whine. Bradshaw's reviews fails utterly in two respects, one it contains too many spoilers not to destroy the experience of the story (so don't read it here if you haven't seen the film yet) and secondly it fails utterly to get the great big gravitational twist at the end (perhaps Mr Bradshaw isn't quite as intellectual a snob as he thinks he is, which might just leave him being a snob!) Three stars Mr Bradshaw does enable you to deliver your normal sneery review but doesn't reflect at all the popularisation of relativity and the beauty of space and science Interstellar makes real on the big screen. Mark Kermode in the Guardian also whines a bit, hey perhaps it's in the contract for journalists joining the paper, talking about plot-holes. The only holes I could spot were worm and black ones, along, of course, with the big one we are digging ourselves as we destroy our ecosystem's ability to support us.Interstellar is epic cinema as its best and it will inspire many people, young and old, to journey deep and long and wide into the wonders of science fact and fiction.**** (Four Stars)

Reviews: Nolan is too ambitious for his own good.
A thrillingly, gloriously flawed film with big ideas that demands to be seen.
main_review: Big budgets and creativity don't often go together. Limitations force us to be creative, to think and plan and dream; effectively unlimited resources too often mean a death to original thinking and problem-solving. Director Christopher Nolan may just be proving himself to be an exception to this rule: his smaller, early films like Memento and The Prestige are creative, intriguing, involving and engaging; all qualities found in mega-budget Inception and the occasion he was handed the reins of that most precious of commercial enterprises, Batman (in the form of his trilogy Batman Begins, The Dark Knight, The Dark Knight Rises). All of these are films which throw spectacle as well as ideas at the viewer, expecting the audience to work as well as be wowed.Interstellar is the synthesis of this, a dizzying spectacle almost impossible to describe or articulate. It's science-fiction set in a future where humanity's food sources are dwindling out- of-control; a solution must be found elsewhere. What follows involves space-travel, space-ships and some very big philosophical and scientific ideas.If all that sounds like the stuff of fan-boy culture, you'd be doing yourself and the film a grave dis-service; the opening act is earth-bound and centred around what becomes the film's key relationship – father-daughter. For all the hyper-reality and wow factor that follows, this is seeking to be a very human story.Watching Interstellar and then trying to form a coherent opinion of it is like trying to self- diagnose after beaten about the head by one of Pacific Rim's gargantuan robots. That's not to suggest the film is clumsy; it's that it's so overwhelming, so expansive, so  big  that you're left grasping for a response that actually does justice to the experience of seeing the film. It's far from perfect – the script is clunky, at times giving in to some laboured plot exposition; it sometimes feels like a blessing that the sound mix is such that some lines are near-drowned out by Hans Zimmer's intense, searing score. That means that the actors don't really shine; especially those with a lot to do. The best performances are more to the fringe than the centre – especially striking is Mackenzie Foy as the 10-year old daughter, carrying an emotionally laden part that's vital to the plot and the especially the film's first third with a disarming ease. Nolan regular Michael Caine is on fine form; Matthew McConaughey struggles gamely with the inadequate script in the central role, and comes up short.The film wants to ask big questions of the nature of reality, belief and existence; questions so big that it's impossible to articulate them properly even in a near-three hour running time. It's also trying to hymn the human capacity for the extraordinary; it does that successfully, with room to spare. For me however, it runs that alongside a deep awareness of humanity's over- arching arrogance, capacity for self-destruction and the ability to ignore that which is self- evident. For all the wonder, the film never feels naive or misty-eyed.In the end, it's an essential, flawed experience; one of the few films that can tip such obvious references to works of the scope of 2001: A Space Odyssey and not seem ridiculous; that's big enough in vision to ignore the lazy temptations of a third-dimension; the reach of which exceeds its grasp but somehow that's all part of the experience, exactly appropriate for what the film is portraying.Christopher Nolan has made many all-round better films, and will make more; but he will not make one that does such full justice to the purpose and experience of cinema as an art form. Neither will he make one as satisfying in its vision despite its failures; nor is it likely that any film, Nolan's or anyone's, will make you feel the way this will. It demands to be seen on a screen big enough to do justice to its ambition and scope.

Reviews: Is this the 2001: A Space Odyssey we wanted but never got?
main_review: So, Interstellar; the latest film from the brilliant and awesome director Christopher Nolan. When Inception? Let's start with the things that don't need mentioning because we know what it's like, the acting is perfect, Matthew McConaughey delivers some fantastic scenes of power and emotion which ultimately takes you all through the movie, you're there for him, you want him to succeed; his daughter as well gives out some pretty surprising scenes, the young actress they got was really good. So on an acting front the film was perfect. this film was in production it was wrapped up in so much secrecy that hardly anyone knew what the plot was about and the cast was kept fairly under wraps too. Anyway what can I say about a three hour space epic from the same guy who made Now do I need to mention the CGI? Nolan tried to use as little as possible and use as much practical effects as he could which worked amazingly well but then when CGI hit your face, you didn't even notice, wow, the visuals of this film are nothing less than stunning, the planets, space, everything looks beautiful.The plot is really what drives a film too, Interstellar is a film which isn't for everyone but it is a unique experience for anyone who watches it. It has some obvious inspiration from 2001: A Space Odyssey but in a good way and it is not a prefect movie in whole. I do have to say it really picks up on the second act, the beginning I felt was quite slow and dragged on a bit and I was hoping it was going to get better, but as soon as they go into the second act it picks up, the story gives you a lot of food for thought, questions that are not very easy to answer and I was definitely thinking about it after the movie ended. Some parts shocked you, some parts will bring you to tears, it is an incredible journey of morals, exploration and desperation.The ending I think will split some people, you either love it or hate it; I look at it positively and loved how they depicted certain physical concepts from science. In the end my opinions on it will probably change with every new thought but I will definitely watch it again which says something.

We spent hours afterwards discussing what happened and what we saw and it's been a long time since. Movie has provoked that response.

Scenario 1: As a serious movie buff:- Someone who scrutinizes a movie with keen observation might found Nolan's new epic space drama lacks a few things. Like,1)A strong script: Interstellar, apart from it's stellar visuals is a hollow one. There isn't anything new that we would expect from the director. 2)Simply isn't Nolan's best work: Nolan had done a lot of home work for this one, which is evident in the production. But, what makes Nolan movies perfect is the twisting, unpredictable storyline. Interstellar is a predictable plot for someone who has common sense 3)Camera works and lighting are not that brilliant: Interstellar, which doesn't have the technical brilliance of last year's Gravity, is not that innovative in the camera department. We were expecting more from a director who made Memento. With all that one may find Interstellar an average flick, if he dared to go deep into the details.Scenario 2:As a science buff:- For someone, who read about black holes and imagined what will it be to travel through one, this movie is priceless. As Nolan's most ambitious work, he spent a lot of time time to make the science right, which made him sacrifice a lot of other elements. Making a movie out of a science book was a great leap in terms of Sci-Fi movies and even though it may not surpass Space Odyssey, it can rest on it's side. Scenario 3: A regular movie goer:- For regular audience, who may look for some eye candy, some good acting and some sentiments, Interstellar is a perfect choice for the weekend.It's brilliant visualization of the unknown, brilliant performances from McConaughey, Chastain, Hathaway and probably everyone on board, marks Interstellar a stellar one. Matt Damon's surprising turn as Mann was also brilliant. As per the scenarios, Interstellar can be labelled as a wonderful cinematic experience other than a brilliant use of arts and artists.....

Reviews: Good space opera, but do NOT see in IMAX
main_review: Though the writing can be criticized, overall it's very watchable. Very notable performance is given by Mackenzie Foy as young Murph. Amusingly, she somehow looks very alike Anne Hathaway who plays Brand.You can pardon it taking liberties with physics. There is no enough fuel on Earth to deliver a spacecraft back from the zone with >0.99c escape velocity (and not enough fuel to slow it down for landing there, in the first place). The enormous time dilation coefficient dictates the escape velocity. But if it gets the plot moving, then OK.I watched it in IMAX 70 mm film projection. IT SUCKED. There was a lot of shutter flicker on bright areas. These days, we don't see the flicker caused the projector shutter (obturator), because modern digital projectors mostly don't need them (though some older digital projectors with sequential colors may have some, but it would be mostly concealed). The image effective sharpness was never better than HD. The editing workflow seems to have been digital, because there was unsharp masking (digital sharpening) fringe always visible. There was AWFUL lot of grain in the picture.Why do they still shoot film these days? Have they ever seen film and digital side by side? It's like 78rpm gramophone disc sounds compared to a CD. Does film grain, tinted colors, lousy sharpness make those old school cinematographers hard? If the movie were shot completely on modern digital cameras, it would have looked MUCH MUCH better.Famous IMAX audio was too loud. The low frequency rumble was so big that it overdrives the ears and causes intermodulation, so that music and speech is heard with tremolo.

Interstellar is a mix of Mind Boggling Visuals, Voice dominant Score, Matthew Mcconaughey's splendid performance and some paradoxical plot holes (which makes movie little flat). But still Nolan's exceptional direction makes it a delight to watch. Nolan's vision on Warm and Black holes and the representing the Gravity and Time in physical dimension is very ostentatious to watch on IMAX screen.I believe this Space Sci-Fi drama needs more humor treatment than quantum physics conversations for PG13 to understand. Change in the Aspect Ratio from 35mm to IMAX 70mm is little disturbing but still it is one of the movies which is larger than life and something which needs dare to attempt. Kudos to Makers.

Reviews: A movie that demands your attention
main_review: Interstellar is definitely quite an experience, particularly in IMAX. I would definitely recommend that people seek it out in the biggest/best format, even though the film does have its share of problems. But still, here we have a nearly three-hour long event movie that is not an action movie, is not based on any existing franchises, features the biggest star of the moment, and is still one of the biggest releases of the year. How can you not check it out?First and foremost, this film is a visual masterpiece. The IMAX photography is simply incredible and really draws you into the picture. I'd say that it's worth seeing the movie for this reason alone. One thing that I appreciated about Interstellar was its relative originality, or at least its creativity. It clearly borrows many concepts and plot elements from other sci-fi establishments (to name a few: 2001, Event Horizon, Aliens, Silent Running) but it combines them in such a way that feels news. The production design is a clear reflection of this, taking our own NASA aesthetic a few steps into the future using cues from these properties. For me, one measure of a sci-fi movie's originality can be found it its robots (in other words, to what extent are they like HAL 9000 or not?), and Interstellar's twin robots TARS and CASE are great characters that I suspect will become iconic in themselves. They have a very cool design and function in the movie; they stole the show at my screening.As is typical of many of Nolan's recent movies, however, the Interstellar's script is a glaring weak link. In many instances, I can forgive its inattention to detail or logic because it is just a vehicle to get Nolan from one set piece to the next, which are often inventive and really engaging. Even the dubious premise washes away after as momentum builds (you might think that a society advanced enough to produce interstellar space travel, artificially intelligent robots, etc. would come up with a better way to harvest food) However, there is just so much bland expository dialogue throughout the movie (which is still explaining itself even in the final scenes) that the 160 minute running time begins to feel like a real chore after not too long. Most of it is completely unnecessary too, as the movie was just trying to be SO BIG that the script just can't manage without adding MORE, MORE, MORE! to the mix. For example, a completely expendable middle act (this plot has like seven acts) starring an un-billed mega-star has no effect on the plot and only exists so that characters can expound at length about the movie's most obvious themes ("Family is important, you guys!") for what feels like 4 hours; an expository parent-teacher conference scene in the first act contains some of the most embarrassing dialogue I've seen all year. The level of self- importance and gravitas that the direction lends to a lot of this dialogue really sucks the fun out of the picture when it boils over into cornball territory every now and then. In comparison to last year's Gravity, another space thriller with a bad script, this film comes across as something between an unfocused mess and an good try that never comes together.Despite any problems with the script or execution, though, there is still a lot to recommend about Interstellar. I think it was definitely oversold and overblown by its exhaustive advertising and by the weight of expectations attached to the Nolan and McConaughey juggernauts, but it is still a really ambitious, good-hearted and non-franchise epic that is more than worthy of being part conversation this year.

Reviews: Lost in space while looking for the volume button
Brilliant visuals and concept but ultimately disappointing
main_review: The sense I really got from the film was that it tried to incorporate too many concepts and story lines into a single film and in the end failed. The greatest flaws were (1) A distinct problem with characterization. For example, Doyle was never even really introduced before his untimely death. His sole purpose was to fuel 'grief' and 'tension' between Conn and Brands – but it failed even at this. For many audiences, they probably never even remembered who Doyle was 5 minutes after his death. Soon after this, Nolan had the chance to redeem himself by showing the toll that 23 years of waiting had on Romilly. Instead, a many who has been in solitude for 23 years shows remarkable sanity. Days later he dies in an explosion that is not only unremarkable but denies the audience a chance of having any empathy for Romilly. Tom, Conns son, is never characterized properly in the first act. Subsequently Nolan attempts to incorporate him with a series of videos from home. It does allow the audience to relate to him somewhat, but this is squandered by a poor foundation. Later on, his relationship with Murph seems shallow and unintimate. He is not even mentioned by Conn when he returns from the tesserect, one begs to ask is Tom even Conns son. I would also say that Mann's character is completely unnecessary and serves little purpose. Nolan has undoubtedly placed Mann in an attempt to portray the thematic concern of humanity's ability for corruption and selfishness. Mann is the fallen knight, the expression of humanity's dark side. Yet the failure of Nolan to really push this thematic concern earlier on really makes Mann's role incongruent to the bigger picture in the movie. Finally Brands relationship with Conn is not realized in any meaningful way. She gives a speech on how Love transcends time – yet this seems contrived and artificial. What's more incongruent is her love with "Edmonds" who we never even see in person and who we can not empathize with in any manner. Furthermore one wonders why Conn chooses to go back to Brands at the ending of the movie; is it friendship or is it love? One surmises it is love; but this is not made clear at all. 2) Nolanfailed to understand Science fiction as a genre. Look at the classics which have really shaped science fiction as a genre. Stanley Kubrick's 2001 A Space Odyssey. One of the keys to Kubrick's film was the black monolith whose role is only implied but never explained. This intrinsic mystery is a facet that is replayed again and again; thick paper cranes in Blade Runner. There was no real sense of mystery in interstellar. Nolan was too technical in his film and attempted to pass fake science as real science. I agree that science fiction utilizes fake science; but almost all film makers either portray the science as completely (1) impossible e.g. Star trek or (2) Possible and believable e.g. Gravity and Gattaca. When you try to explain real science – do it properly or don't do it at all. The science of Interstellar would have been acceptable if Nolan had simply not gone to great lengths to explain it to the audience and make it seem real. OVERALL impressions - quite disappointing from Nolan. Too many ideas and characters and not enough coherence to really make it a profound film.

Reviews: It's not possible. No, it's necessary.
main_review: Interstellar is a movie about two things: An attempt to save mankind and also a pledge to return to your family. It's as gripping as it gets.Nolan wants to show us that no matter how hard you try in order to help others it's always the ones that you hold dearest that will feel most hurt if you don't get pull through.The movie is a gorgeous depiction of an unbelievable galaxy that feels understandable yet not present. It's also a movie about desperation, an attempt to save something that is doomed to fail and making that the absolute essence of work and dedication.Nolan has accomplished something special in both this movie and Inception (2010) - his usage and adaptation of time. Time is as key in the both movies but with different narratives. This movie speaks more about the choices we make, while Inception deals with a fundamental questioning concerning our perception of reality.It's a stellar performance, an incredible movie! Emotional and inspirational!

main_review: Let me just say it: Interstellar is the greatest movie ever made. Period. I've watched it over 200 times-yes, two hundred-and not only do I cry every single time like it's my first watch, but for some strange reason, it also makes me insanely hungry for hot dogs. I don't know if it's the intense emotional gravity of the baseball scene when the grandfather says he missed hotdogs at baseball games, the beautiful score, or if my soul just associates wormholes with grilled meat... but that's what happens. Nolan makes me weep and crave mustard. That's power.Let's start with the obvious: Christopher Nolan didn't direct a movie-he carved a masterpiece into the fabric of time itself. From the first scene, Interstellar grabs you with its dusty, fading Earth and pulls you into a journey that's not just about space-it's about love, sacrifice, humanity, and the terrifying beauty of the unknown.Matthew McConaughey as Cooper? My God. That man acted. He didn't play a character, he became every father who ever had to make the unthinkable choice: leave your child to save their future. That scene where he watches Murph grow up through those video messages-are you kidding me? It shattered me. I'm not talking "tears down the cheek" crying-I'm talking full body, grab-a-pillow, ugly-sobbing like someone just broke up with me through a voicemail from Saturn.And Murph-Jessica Chastain brought so much depth and raw emotion that it made the entire concept of time dilation feel personal. That ticking clock on the water planet wasn't just some sci-fi gimmick. It was every second you missed with your loved ones. And Hans Zimmer? That soundtrack doesn't just set the mood-it punches your heart into the fifth dimension.The visuals? Unreal. Space has never looked so poetic. The black hole-Gargantua-was scientifically accurate and emotionally devastating. It's a cosmic monster and a metaphor for everything we can't understand about time, love, and existence. And don't even get me started on that ending. People debate it all the time, but for me? It was perfect. Nolan didn't just tie it up with a neat bow-he pulled it through a tesseract of hope, forgiveness, and faith in the human spirit.Now let's talk hot dogs, because at this point, it's part of my Interstellar ritual. I can't explain it. I sit down to watch Cooper blast off into the stars and suddenly I'm like, "Where's the ketchup?!" Maybe it's a subconscious association-like my brain saying, "You're about to get emotionally wrecked, better get something comforting." Or maybe it's because every time I watch it, I feel like a little kid again, watching something bigger than myself, and nothing says childhood wonder like hot dogs and mind-blowing cosmic theories or like I said before, it could be the baseball scene when the grandfather says he wanted a hotdog.Also, let's not overlook the quiet brilliance of the robots-TARS and CASE. They had more personality than half the human characters in most sci-fi movies. Sarcasm settings? Adjustable honesty? A rectangular hunk of AI steel had me laughing and crying. That's elite-level storytelling.Here's the bottom line: Interstellar is a movie about love being a force greater than time and space. It dares to ask big questions, and instead of answering them with explosions or aliens, it answers with human emotion, scientific wonder, and the idea that maybe-just maybe-what binds us across galaxies isn't just gravity... but love.So yeah. Interstellar is the only movie that's made me cry 200 times and crave hot dogs like I'm at a baseball game inside a wormhole. And I wouldn't change a thing.If this movie isn't the best of all time, I don't know what is. Nothing else makes you feel small in the universe and infinite in love, all in the same breath.

Like everybody else back then. Of course, he didn't start that way." And then Cooper's crash scene flashback. I loved the fact that I didn't have any idea what was going on - yet. I loved the element of mystery and suspense that the movie sustained in the beginning and throughout.Quite a few reviews have already mentioned Hans Zimmer's beautiful soundtracks for Interstellar. It would be a gross understatement to say that the haunting music touched my heart and brought tears to my eyes. Even though Interstellar is a pretty fantastic movie on its own, the effect it had on me would have been only about 50% of what it is now without the brilliant score.Interstellar's visual effects also deserve a special mention. The enormous waves on Miller's planet and the stunningly ominous black hole succeeding in sending shivers down my spine. Hats off to Paul Franklin (visual effects supervisor), and to Christopher Nolan for minimizing the use of CGI to create as realistic an experience for the audience as possible.The storyline revolves around a strong father-daughter relationship, which I could relate to on a personal level. Some are critical about how Interstellar seems to throw in the 'love conquers all' cliche at the last minute for no apparent reason. Actually, if you think about it, love was always the main theme of Interstellar - be it the love between Cooper and Murph or the bond between Amelia Brand and Dr. Edmunds. It was Cooper's bond with his daughter that enabled him to transmit to her across space and time the secret quantum data necessary for Plan A to work. It is a fact that director Christopher Nolan did not reveal to Hans Zimmer that Interstellar was a science-fiction film in the beginning. Instead, he maintained that the film was about the bond between a father and his son. Hans Zimmer probably related to this because he himself has a son. The score for Interstellar, which I know has attracted universal appeal, might not have been quite as good if the director had revealed the rest of the storyline!The movie itself may have been nearly three hours long, but I felt completely engaged throughout. I felt like I was with all of the characters during their plight and adventure, and like I was traversing light years like they were. The movie was almost nonstop action from Miller's planet all the way to the 'powered slingshot around the black hole' , which made it all the more thrilling to watch.Lastly, the acting was convincing enough to make the events in the story believable. Matthew McConaughey does a really good job during quite a number of scenes, especially when he is witnessing the 'years of messages', crying out to Murph when he is trapped inside the tesseract and during the end, when he finally reunites with his elderly daughter. I liked both Mackenzie Foy as little Murph and Jessica Chastain as the older Murph. I feel that Amelia Brand wasn't given much of a character in the first place, but nevertheless Anne Hathaway does the job well enough.Words cannot describe my feelings as I exited the theater that night. It is hardly sufficient to say that it was a weird kind of exhilaration. No movie has ever made me feel that way before, and probably never will. Interstellar is so unique in so many different ways. I sincerely hope that this movie has had a similar effect on many young people, like myself. Watching it for the first time was a thrilling, life-changing experience that I will thankfully never forget.

Habits shape our daily lives more than we realize. From the moment we wake up to the time we go to bed, our actions are largely governed by routines we've built over time. Whether it's brushing our teeth, checking our phones, or grabbing a cup of coffee, these small, seemingly insignificant behaviors accumulate and define who we are. Understanding the power of habit can help us harness it to achieve personal growth, productivity, and overall well-being.What Are Habits?Habits are automatic behaviors triggered by specific cues. Psychologists describe habits as loops consisting of three main parts: cue, routine, and reward. The cue is what triggers the behavior, the routine is the action itself, and the reward is what reinforces the habit. For example, feeling tired in the afternoon (cue) might lead to drinking coffee (routine), which results in increased alertness (reward). Over time, this loop becomes ingrained in the brain, making the habit difficult to break.The brain develops habits to save energy. If every action required conscious effort, we'd be mentally exhausted by midday. Instead, the brain automates repetitive behaviors so we can focus on new challenges. This is why habits, once formed, can be difficult to change-but also why they can be incredibly powerful when used effectively.The Science Behind Habit FormationResearch suggests that habits form through a process called neuroplasticity, where the brain's neural pathways strengthen with repetition. The more we perform a habit, the stronger the connections become. This is why breaking bad habits or forming new ones requires consistent effort.Studies show that it takes about 21 to 66 days for a new habit to become automatic, depending on its complexity and the individual. Simple habits, like drinking a glass of water in the morning, may take a few weeks, while more complex ones, like exercising daily, might take months.How Small Habits Lead to Big ChangesOne of the most powerful aspects of habits is their ability to compound over time. Small daily improvements-just 1% better each day-can lead to massive transformation over months or years. This idea, popularized by James Clear in Atomic Habits, is based on the principle of compound interest applied to personal development.For example, if you start by reading just one page of a book per day, you'll have read dozens of books in a year. If you do five minutes of exercise daily, it can eventually turn into a full workout routine. Small habits create momentum, making it easier to sustain positive changes.Breaking Bad HabitsJust as good habits can improve our lives, bad habits can hold us back. Breaking a bad habit requires disrupting the cue-routine-reward cycle. Some effective strategies include:
1. Identify the Cue - Recognizing what triggers the habit is the first step. Is it stress, boredom, or a specific time of day?2. Replace the Routine - Instead of trying to eliminate the habit outright, replace it with a healthier alternative. His job brings him into the homes of various customers, from the wealthy elite to the struggling middle class, each representing different facets of Filipino society. It highlights how cable television, once a luxury, has become a necessity for many, serving as a means of escape from the harsh realities of life. The film subtly questions the value society places on entertainment versus real-life struggles, emphasizing how people use television to distract themselves from their personal and financial hardships.The film also touches on the plight of blue-collar workers, emphasizing the lack of job security, unfair labor practices, and the physical toll of such work. Through Mando's character, the film sheds light on the sacrifices of workers who provide essential services but are often underappreciated and underpaid.Another critical theme is generational conflict. The film's cinematography captures the essence of Manila's urban landscape, from its congested streets to its towering buildings. The visuals are raw, with a documentary-like feel, immersing viewers in Mando's daily struggles.The use of natural lighting and handheld shots adds to the film's authenticity, making it feel like an intimate portrait of a man caught in an unforgiving system. The contrast between the different households Mando visits is also visually striking, reinforcing the stark inequalities within the city.### **Performance and Character Development**The lead actor delivers a poignant performance as Mando, embodying the fatigue and resilience of a man trying to keep up with a rapidly changing world. His portrayal is understated yet deeply affecting, making the audience sympathize with his plight. The supporting cast, including the son, customers, and fellow workers, contribute to the film's realism by portraying everyday people with distinct struggles and aspirations.Each character Mando encounters adds depth to the narrative, making it not just his story but a collective reflection of Filipino society. Reviews: A Flawed, but Solid Space Odyssey from Christopher Nolan
main_review: With many people split on this film, I can say that I'm in the middle. For starters, I love this premise of humans having to find another planet for relocation. Many of the scientific aspects of the movie are fascinating, from worm holes to black holes to relativity of time. However, aside from the subtle environmental message to not ruin the Earth (which is rarely done in cinema) Christopher Nolan did more tell than show this time around. This can make you get easily get lost if you're not paying enough attention, especially considering that this movie is almost 3 hours (which fortunately never drags. Unfortunately this makes most of the characters less identifiable and interesting and more there to explain the exposition (whether of their own background or of the plot). The upside however is that all of their respectable actors giving great performances that do manage to win you over emotionally in one or two scenes despite their lack of identifiable traits for most other scenes. I didn't care as much for the individual astronaut's survival because I became so attached to them as much because I wanted Matthew McConaughey's daughter to survive (their relationship was actually pretty good) as well as the rest of humanity since time is running out. The soundtrack is a great boost to the also visuals of this film, which are amazing in imagery and atmosphere. This is especially true in the space scenes but did lack creativity in the planet scenes. Without giving away any major spoilers, the climax is the most exciting and interesting part of the film until the confusing and somewhat disappointing scene at the end that could have given us a bit more of a payoff (though that could be done in a possible sequel). Overall, while I thought that there could have been improvements in character depth and the "show don't tell" motif, the intriguing concept, tense story line, pretty visuals boosted by a soothing musical score, and effective acting are enough for me to give this a positive regard.

Christopher Nolan's Interstellar is a visually stunning and emotionally resonant science fiction epic that blends cutting-edge science with profound human themes. Set in a dystopian future where Earth faces ecological collapse, the film follows astronaut Cooper (Matthew McConaughey) and a team of scientists as they journey through a wormhole to find a new home for humanity. With the guidance of theoretical physicist Kip Thorne, Nolan crafts a scientifically grounded narrative that explores complex concepts like black holes, time dilation, and relativity, while also diving deep into the emotional core of human relationships-particularly the bond between Cooper and his daughter, Murph. The film's breathtaking cinematography, combined with Hans Zimmer's haunting score and McConaughey's powerful performance, creates a poignant meditation on love, sacrifice, and the relentless pursuit of survival. Though the film's ambitious narrative and intricate science may challenge some viewers, Interstellar remains a thought-provoking and unforgettable cinematic journey, solidifying Nolan's reputation as one of modern cinema's most visionary filmmakers.

Interstellar: A Cosmic Odyssey of Love and Loss
Christopher Nolan's "Interstellar" is not just a science fiction film; it's a profound exploration of human existence, the power of love, and the enduring spirit of hope in the face of impending doom. Set in a dystopian future where Earth faces imminent environmental collapse, the film follows a group of astronauts on a perilous mission to find a new home for humanity among the stars.At the heart of "Interstellar" lies a poignant portrayal of father-daughter love. Matthew McConaughey delivers a stellar performance as Cooper, a former pilot turned farmer, grappling with the responsibility of leaving his children behind to embark on a potentially one-way journey. The emotional core of the film resonates deeply, exploring themes of sacrifice, regret, and the enduring bonds of family. Anne Hathaway shines as Dr. Brand, a brilliant scientist driven by a unwavering belief in humanity's future. Their dynamic, while occasionally fraught with tension, ultimately fuels the mission and provides a sense of human connection amidst the vast, impersonal cosmos.Nolan masterfully blends hard science with philosophical musings, creating a visually stunning and intellectually stimulating cinematic experience. The film delves into complex scientific concepts like relativity, wormholes, and black holes, presenting them in a way that is both accessible and awe-inspiring. The visual effects are breathtaking, particularly the depiction of Gargantua, a supermassive black hole, and the mesmerizing portrayal of time dilation. The soundtrack, composed by Hans Zimmer, is equally impressive, soaring and melancholic, perfectly capturing the film's emotional depth and cosmic grandeur.However, "Interstellar" is not without its flaws. Some may find the pacing uneven, with certain segments feeling slower than others. The ending, while emotionally resonant, may leave some viewers feeling unsatisfied or unconvinced by its resolution. Additionally, the film's reliance on deus ex machina moments, particularly in the final act, might detract from the overall sense of realism.Despite these minor shortcomings, "Interstellar" remains a cinematic masterpiece. It's a film that stays with you long after the credits roll, prompting reflection on profound questions about our place in the universe, the importance of human connection, and the enduring power of hope. Nolan's ambitious vision, coupled with stellar performances and breathtaking visuals, creates an unforgettable cinematic experience that transcends the boundaries of science fiction."Interstellar" is a testament to the power of storytelling to explore the deepest human emotions and inspire wonder about the cosmos. It's a film that will continue to captivate audiences for years to come, reminding us of our resilience, our capacity for love, and the unwavering human spirit that drives us to reach for the stars.

main_review: "I'm not afraid of death. ... I'm afraid of time."Space and time. Faith and science. Complacency and proactivity. Lie and sacrifice. Reality and artistic depiction.---Imagine making time the antagonist of your film. Christopher Nolan takes you through a mesmerizing cosmic dance of space and time bearing witness to humanity's best and worst instincts for survival. With an IMAX Digital 4K projector on a gigantic screen that quite literally covers an entire wall and a 12-channel sound system that can mimic the rumblings of a spacecraft traversing an incomprehensible dimension inside the theater accompanied by a score by Hans Zimmer produced mainly with a church organ, the film transports you to a barren yet hypnotizingly beautiful landscape near a supermassive black hole where you find yourself rolling a die on the fate of the human species. There's ethical and philosophical questions about what it means to be a sacrifice and the lengths one can or should go to survive. Throughout all this, the film somehow manages to keep a focus on the humanity and the human scale of time.You can criticize it for the several artistic liberties they've taken to craft a story but I feel a lot of it is justified except maybe for the very last scene which is slightly debatable imho. Even then, I can understand that they were just trying to tie a narrative thread at the very end. It's a leap of faith--a suspension of disbelief.This is the greatest cinematic experience I've ever had in my life. It's crafted specifically for IMAX and is meant to be experienced in an IMAX theater. I can't even imagine what the true best IMAX experience with 70 mm film at the approximate resolution of 18K would be like.

main_review: Interstellar is one of the greatest films of all time. I had the chance to revisit it in theaters for its tenth anniversary, and it couldn't have been more fitting. Films simply aren't made the way they used to be: casting once revolved around genuine talent rather than "woke" agendas, and scripts were crafted with real passion rather than quick-and-easy crowd appeal, as we often see on streaming platforms today.Watching it again, I uncover new details and grow in appreciation each time. The story feels increasingly relevant to our current reality, despite having been conceived long ago. Its ability to balance science, emotion, and grand-scale spectacle reminds us how small we are in the vastness of the universe, yet how deeply our choices can resonate. Interstellar remains a remarkable testament to a bygone era of filmmaking-one that deserves to be cherished and revisited.

Reviews: Finally IMDB reviews that recognize prime Sci Fi
main_review: I am gratified to see a general rating here of almost 9 stars. While this movie is a mind-twister at times and doesn't tie all the strings together (nor does it try to), the concept, production, music, special effects, directing, acting and basic plot are all superb. Even the ending was well-done, with just enough mystery to leave the viewer delightedly wanting more.This film has everything. I don't want to say too much about it due to spoilers. If one hasn't seen it yet, understand this is cerebral fiction. It challenges your mind and doesn't answer all the questions, nor does it have to. It doesn't tie everything up with a nice pretty bow, but leaves the viewer to further explore possibilities in our imaginations... and amazingly does so without leaving us hanging in the air as with so many other films.Superb film making. I give it 9 because near the end it goes so cerebral it almost jumps the shark (not quite) and soars over the head of many viewers. Nevertheless it pulls things back together in a somewhat unexpected way, leaving the viewer both wanting more, but contented with what is presented. And it does so by putting the FICTION in science without losing the science in the process. That is quite an unusual story-telling feat.This is how science fiction should be made.

Let me get this straight-this movie is a cinematic MASTERPIECE. The story, the music and score, the acting...everything is SO WELL DONE. In my personal opinion Matthew McConaughey completely carried this movie. He delivered such a remarkable and jaw dropping performance that left me speechless at the end. Are we even going to talk about the scene where he watches the videos from his kids?! I was in awe-and honestly a little unsettled-the whole scene because of how real his performance felt, as if he truly was a father mourning the lost years of his kids' lives, like Cooper. The way he could tap into such raw emotion, make himself cry, and deliver such an eerily authentic portrayal was almost frightening in its realism. He also had such a great onscreen bond with Mckenzie Foy that even left me in tears as we watched their relationship and bond unfold and eventually save humanity. There were many aha! Moments and the adrenaline was indeed pumping as I was mesmerized and pulled deeply into concentration on the movie.So why is this movie missing two stars? Don't get me wrong Christopher Nolan completely delivered and made me feel all the emotions he wanted viewers to feel, and while I did enjoy it, it is not a movie to take lightly. There is a lot of informational thrown at you and a lot of words the average movie watcher might not understand. I get it, it's a sci-fi movie, and a great one at that, but the end completely messed with my brain and had me scavaging the internet and Youtube for explanations. Because of this, I feel like this movie is one that you really can't talk to your friends while watching or get up to go to the bathroom since you will miss critical information. Also, there were some scenes and monologues that felt a little too long and didn't do much to drive the story forward.Overall, I thoroughly enjoyed Interstellar. It's an incredibly captivating and emotional film that kept me hooked from start to finish. While it can be a bit confusing at times and definitely a lot to take in, I would absolutely recommend it to anyone who loves thought-provoking, visually stunning movies.
